standard.title: Analyse how language positions listeners
standard.description: listen to spoken texts that have different purposes and audiences, analysing how language features position listeners to respond in particular ways, and use interacting skills to present and discuss opinions regarding these texts
standard.prior_knowledge: Students use interaction skills to discuss and present ideas, evaluating features of spoken texts (AC9E7LY02). They have not yet analysed how language features specifically position listeners — the mechanism through which spoken texts direct response.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students listen to spoken texts, analyse how language features position listeners to respond in particular ways, and use interaction skills to present and discuss opinions about those texts.

nodes.label: How language positions listeners
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify language features in a spoken text that position listeners toward particular responses and explain the positioning mechanism.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two language features in a spoken text (e.g. inclusive pronouns, emotive language, stereotypes) and explain how each positions the listener to respond in a particular way.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how language features in spoken texts — including stereotype creation, emotive language and speaker positioning devices — direct listeners toward particular responses.
wider: Compare how the same topic is positioned differently for listeners in two spoken texts from different contexts (e.g. a community radio program versus a commercial broadcast)
Examine how podcasts use para-linguistic features alongside language to create intimacy and position the listener as an in-group member

response_modes.reason: The mechanism of positioning — how a language feature makes a listener more likely to respond in a particular way — is abstract. Students need a reasoning scaffold: feature → mechanism → listener effect. Without this chain, students describe the feature without explaining the positioning.

success_criteria: Student identifies a language feature in a spoken text
Student explains how that feature positions the listener — naming the expected or likely response it encourages
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot explain the positioning mechanism of a language feature cannot present a grounded opinion about a spoken text at N2 — they can only describe the text, not analyse how it acts on listeners.

nodes.label: Presenting and discussing opinions about spoken texts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use interaction skills to present and discuss opinions about spoken texts, including speaking clearly, presenting a reasoned opinion and responding to others.
nodes.minimum_width: Present an opinion about a spoken text, including at least one specific language feature as evidence, speaking clearly for an appropriate length of time.
nodes.typical_width: Use effective dialogue and discussion strategies in formal and informal contexts — presenting opinions about spoken texts with specific evidence, listening to and responding to others' views, and speaking with clarity and appropriate pacing.
wider: Conduct a formal discussion of a spoken text using structured dialogue protocols, evaluating how the structure itself affects the quality of opinion exchange
Compare how the same opinion about a text lands differently when presented orally versus in writing — examining what the spoken mode adds or limits

response_modes.reason: Oral discussion skills require repeated practice under real discussion conditions. The skills — speaking clearly, responding to others, maintaining coherence under conversational pressure — develop through practice, not conceptual extension.

success_criteria: Student presents an opinion about a spoken text with at least one specific piece of evidence
Student demonstrates at least one interaction skill (e.g. responding to another's view, inviting others' contributions, building on a point)
